title: Meditation - Revisiting the Basics
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up Pema Chodron's book How to Meditate: A Practical Guide to Making Friends with Your Mind, reading it as a tune-up for the basics of Seishu's own sitting. Seishu returns often to coming back to the breath, and tells of a 1970s group therapy marathon where Seishu realized having heard nothing the partner said. Seishu describes learning to accept sleepiness during a seven-day Samish sesshin, after which the worst part was being upset about it. Seishu then tries four of her suggestions: a longer body scan, a check of emotions and thoughts, watching breath and body with the storyline dropped, and making brushing teeth or walking one block the object of attention.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's word.*
Well, good evening, everybody.
It's great to see you.
It's a pretty decent turnout for when you have the Zoom alternative.
And Scott, it's good to see you on Zoom.
So welcome.
Tonight I'm going to talk about meditation.
After all, it is the foundation of our practice.
A lot of what I'm going to say comes from this book, How to Meditate: A Practical Guide to Making Friends with Your Mind by Pema Chodron.
That's a pretty good idea, to make friends with your mind, I think, because if you don't, there'll be a lot of trouble.
This winter practice period, Talus and I taught the Intro to Zen class.
First of all, I wanted to say thank you, Talus, because I really enjoyed working with you and I learned a lot from the things you presented in the class, so I really appreciate it.

After class, I got an email from one of the participants who made some comments about the class, but he also said that he had been reading this book, and it was very helpful to his meditation practice.
Now, I've always liked Pema Chodron.
I think she's an excellent writer and writes very clearly about things that are hard to write about.
She often has very good practical advice for how to bring meditation practice into our day-to-day lives, and I very much appreciate that.
So I thought it was probably a good idea for me to read this book and see what I've been doing all these years, and how it compares to the things that she recommends.
I found it very helpful.

There were some things that were new to me that I really hadn't heard before, some new ways of doing things, and even with the things that I had heard before, some of them I had just forgotten and wasn't doing.
So it really gave my meditation practice a nice tune up.
What I thought I'd do tonight is go over some of the themes in the book that I appreciated, and then some of the practical suggestions that she has that I've been trying out for the last month or so.
Of course, any meditation book starts out with posture.
There's some information about sitting in a chair, sitting on a cushion, and having a stable upright posture.
So much of meditation is a body practice, and I always like being reminded that it's so important to pay attention to your body.

Then she talks about when you're starting out, but I think really, even if you've been at it a really long time, it's important to set some realistic goals for yourself: how long are you going to meditate each day?
When are you going to do it?
Where are you going to do it?
And then stick to it.
This practice takes self-discipline.
Then one of the main themes she talks about is to develop an attitude of kindness towards yourself and whatever you're experiencing.
We all want to have a peaceful, comfortable, meaningful meditation practice or meditation experience, but it doesn't happen that way very often.
It really does require a change of attitude.
We have to drop our preferences for some things and our resistances to other things, and accept what actually happens.

Imagine if you could develop the ability to just observe and notice achy knees, or a jumpy mind, or a painful memory or emotion, to be able to notice instead of all the things we add: a storyline, a tense body, judgments about "I shouldn't be feeling this way, I shouldn't be thinking this."
So she has a quote about being kind to yourself and accepting what your experience is.
*The tendency to be critical, to be hard on ourselves does not come from Buddha nature, which is the basic goodness within all of us.
It comes from our ego and from our conditioning.
We all have the seeds of goodness, and we need to nourish them.*
We train in attention, but it's friendly attention.
So be kind to yourself, whatever you experience in meditation, and curious about what you encounter.
Another point that she makes frequently in the book is the importance of coming back again and again and again, 10,000 times, to the body and to the breath and to the present moment.
We're more likely to be critical of distraction than we are to acknowledge the importance of recognizing it and coming back to the breath.
We're so prone to not paying attention to each moment of our lives.
I just think that's human nature.
But the important thing is that you've noticed it and that you've returned to the present moment.
Have you ever had the experience, on a long driving trip, where you go 10, 20, 30 miles, and you realize, "I haven't been paying attention at all to my drive"?
Maybe enough so that I didn't have an accident, but I have no memory of the scenery I passed, and I went, "Where was I in the last 20 or 30 miles?"
Or how about paying attention when you're having a conversation, or listening in a class?
How hard is it to listen for a whole class?
I had a very powerful lesson about listening when I was in my mid 20s.
This is long before I started to meditate.
I signed up for a group therapy marathon.
I don't know if they do these things anymore.
This was the early 1970s.
It had a schedule like a weekend meditation retreat: it started on Friday afternoon, went into the evening, all day Saturday into the evening, all day Sunday.
The first exercise they had us do, we're in this whole group, and then they split us into pairs.
The assignment was for person A to spend one or two minutes telling person B a little bit about themselves.
After they were done, the roles would be switched.
So we did that.
We came back into the whole group, and then the leader said, "Now what I want is for the first listener, person B, to tell the group a little bit about what your partner said to you."
I was the first person that had to do that.
Until I realized that I had not.
When my partner was telling me about herself, I was thinking about what I was going to say to her, and I had heard virtually nothing of what she said.
I was terribly embarrassed.
I couldn't do anything.
I had no idea.
I'd never had an experience like that before.
The only thing I could do was just confess: "I'm sorry, I wasn't listening, I was thinking of what I was going to say."
But it was a very good lesson.
I never forgot it.
I have improved since then as a listener, but there are still times in a conversation when my mind is somewhere else.
And coming back is the only option.
It's something to recognize when we're able to do that.
In one part of the book, someone talks about research that some neuroscientists have done.
They put experienced meditators in an MRI machine so that their brain function showed up on a graph.

What they found was that when the meditators went on automatic pilot, got lost in thought, or were escalating emotionally, their brain functions showed up as a deep groove, and as they continued to do that, the groove got deeper.
So these repetitive patterns are hard to break.
But what they also found is that when the meditators caught it, and they paused, and they realized they were escalating on their own automatic pilot, a different groove was established in the brain.
So that tells us that when you pause and you notice a habitual pattern, you're establishing a new pathway in the brain.
Here it is, science confirming how important it is to recognize that you've been distracted or lost, and then to come back to the present moment.
So that's one thing.
Another thing that she talks about frequently is seeing each moment of your life just as it is, with nothing added, and seeing yourself just as you are, with nothing added.
So whether you're tired, relaxed, wound up, distracted, or joyful.
And here's a quote from her:
*Meditation accepts us just as we are, in both our tantrums and bad habits, in our love and commitments and happiness.
It allows us to have a more flexible identity, because we learn to accept ourselves and all of our human experience with more tenderness and openness.
We learn to accept the present moment with an open heart.*
So everything in your life, every moment, every struggle is the path for awakening.
Everything is an opportunity for that.
And I don't know where I read this, but I read somewhere the suggestion that we try to be like the sky.
The vast sky accepts all weather, without complaint and without resistance.
It has infinite patience.
Today, raining, cloudy all day long, the sky didn't mind a bit.
I did, but the sky didn't.
It's so common for us to be critical of ourselves when we're distracted.
Our judgments are extra, and they're just extra suffering.
So again and again, Pema Chodron says, accept your situation, whatever it is, make friends with it.
I know Thich Nhat Hanh has said that we ought to treat our anger like a little brother: take him by the hand, gently, and offer him some tea.
And in the book What Is Zen by Norman Fischer and Susan Moon, he talks about zazen, meditation, as sitting in the awareness of being alive, being present with the basic human experience.
The basic human experience includes all the struggles we add and create.
So notice them with kindness.
Now, in the past when I meditated, I used to tell myself that I really didn't like being sleepy.
That was my least favorite thing.
I would say to myself, "I'd rather be in pain, because at least when I'm in pain, I'm alert."
Then one week at our Samish sesshin that goes seven days, I didn't sleep well for the whole time.
So I was sleepy every day for the entire retreat.
I don't know how this happened, but at some point I actually stopped being upset about it, and I just accepted it.
That made a big difference.
It actually made it okay to be sleepy.
I used to think that when I was sleepy, I was sleepy all the time, but I noticed, "I'm sleepy," and then I'd have these moments where I was quite alert.
Then I'd be sleepy again, and then quite alert again, and then sleepy again.
I just went back and forth like that all day, but it was different than I thought it was.
I also discovered that the worst thing about being sleepy was being upset about being sleepy.
Once I was okay with it, it was okay.
And now I prefer being sleepy to being in pain.
I'm going to go over about four practical suggestions that Pema makes in the book that I found interesting and helpful.
The first thing she talks about, once you've established your meditation posture, is to do a thorough physical inventory.
Go through your whole body, part by part: from your feet, your legs, your knees, your upper legs, your buttocks, your genitals, your chest, your back, everything, head to toe.
Take about one or two minutes to do that.
All you're trying to do is notice how you feel.
That's all.
I had been doing an abbreviated version of that.
I might spend 30 seconds just noticing.
When I took one or two minutes, I noticed that I often had a little tension in my shoulders that I had missed with the real quick checking, and I could just drop that and let that tension go.
So it was helpful to take a longer period of time to check on how my body felt.
It reminded me of Mel Weitsman once saying, "Let your shoulders fall, your shoulders don't hold you up."
I've always liked that because I carry a lot in my shoulders.
Then she also recommends doing the same thing with emotions and thoughts at the beginning of meditation.
What does the mind do at the start of meditation?
Are you aware of any emotions that you're feeling?
If so, is there a place in your body where you notice this?
We're not trying to change anything.
You're just trying to notice whatever your emotional or mental state is.
It's okay.
No judgment.
We are just establishing awareness of what is right now, this life, this moment.

Then another very helpful suggestion I found is that if during meditation, or any time off the cushion, you notice a powerful emotion, she had a very specific couple of suggestions for how to deal with it.
She said to go immediately to the body and take three or four deep breaths and pay some attention to that.
Then find the place in your body where you're most aware of the feeling and put some attention there.
So you're watching both your breath and the place in your body.
Then drop the storyline that goes with the feeling: who's at fault, what was done to you, what you're going to do or what you wish you'd done.
Drop all of that, and just give the feeling in your body and your breath some attention and watch it.
Because emotion without the storyline is energy, and if you just watch the energy, it'll move and change.
I found that very helpful because what I have been doing when I have a strong feeling, or not a strong feeling, is pretty much just watching my breath.
I wasn't paying much attention to the place.
I dropped the storyline, but I wasn't paying attention to the place in my body where the feeling resided, and it was very helpful to do both.
So you watch the breath and pay attention to the emotion without the storyline.
I appreciate that.
Then the last helpful suggestion I will go over is that she suggested we take a daily activity, especially something that you do every day, and make it the object of meditation.
We all have dozens and dozens of things we do every day, but you could take a simple thing like brushing your teeth.
Be aware of the taste of the toothpaste.
Be aware of the brush moving on your gums and your teeth, and the feeling of holding the handle and moving your hand.
You can do it with washing dishes: can I put away the dishes with my full attention?
I walk a lot, so I would often ask, can I walk one block and just pay attention to what my senses pick up, what I hear, what I see, what I smell?
Or can I pay attention for one block to my body moving, to lifting my foot and putting my foot down?
What all that did was [unclear: "see what I put here"].
That just reminded me of how hard it is.
That's amazing.
You pick any activity that you do all the time and it's hard to pay attention even for two minutes of brushing.
So that gets back to how important it is to come back over and over and over again.
And because I have this history of a listening problem, I would ask, how long can I listen to this person before I get distracted?
And when I do, can I come back?
That's a wonderful exercise to do whether you're on the phone or you're talking to someone in person.

With the things I do regularly, I tend to get into a routine, whether it's mowing the lawn or [unclear: "better dating"], and I was definitely in a routine with my meditation: sit down and set my posture and do my quick check-in and that sort of thing.
I just found it very helpful to look at all of the suggestions she had and try some things.
It gave my meditation practice, both on and off the cushion, a really [unclear: "nice to"].
So that's what I wanted to share with you tonight.
I think that's all I have [unclear: "to solve that"] I prepared to say.
I'm sure we have time, because I tend to give short talks, I'm sure we have time for questions or comments.
And so what do I do to turn off the.
And then we'll do the chat after I turn off the recording.
